articles.text: Monday's receipts of cattle in the Chicago yards amounted to 7,000 head, against 14,000 received the previous Monday. The quality of the cattle was rather poor, only a few car-loads of extra choice Christmas beeves selling for more than $5. Some 940 lb. Nebraska yearlings sold at $4, while a bunch of 1,520 lb. steers brought the same price; showing a vast difference in quality.
articles.summary: Chicago cattle receipts on Monday were 7,000 head, half the previous Monday's, and of poor quality.

articles.text: The question of changing the exemption laws at the next session of the legislature is now being discussed by the terrtorial press and it is a noble comcomment on their honesty and devotion to public good that it is practically a unit in favor of change. At present, besides his homestead, library, wearing apparel and household goods in store, every resident can claim $1,500 worth of property as exempt from any debt unless secured by mortgage. To a certain extent, we believe thoroughly in exemptions but the $1.500 limit is too high by at least $1,200. It furnishes a means of refusal of payment for every dishonest rascal who can secure a cent credit. Not only is it a means of swindling constantly employed by dishonest men to beat their creditors, but it is a positive detriment to the honest man, who, when he gets credit, is generally compelled to pay an exorbitant rate of interest, due solely to these large exemption laws. A total abolishment of the exemption laws would be far preferable to the present ones, and we certainly hope to see them repealed or the amount greatly lessened at the coming session of the legislature.
articles.summary: Editorial urging the territorial legislature to repeal or sharply reduce the $1,500 debt exemption.

articles.text: What future benefits may accure to the dairymen from the passage of the oleomargarine bill can only be conjectured, but it must be confessed that thus far no very gratifying results have followed the enactment of that measure. A comparison of present prices with those of a year ago shows scarcely an appreciable difference so far as creamery butter is concerned, while dairy is barely 1@2c higher than then. And it is a question whether the moderate advance in the latter is not more the result of the drought which prevailed through the dairy districts of the west during the last season, than of any restrictions upon the manufacture and sale of the imitation article. That the staple has not reached anywhere near as high a point as the trade generally expected, can not be ascribed to the fact that most other food articles are cheaper than a year ago, for we find that cheese is fully 3 cents per pound higher than at the corresponding time last year, notwithstanding the fact that the export demand has taken out of the country more than 200,000 boxes less than during the season of 1885.—[U. S. Produce Review.
articles.summary: Reprint from the U.S. Produce Review saying the oleomargarine law has done little so far to raise butter prices.

articles.headline: Some More Old-Timers.
articles.text:
Al. Gifford is married and living in Miles City.

Miss Mary Brophy is at home in Mingusville.

A. W. Merrifield is in his old Canadian home and will return in the spring.

Wm. Paddock and wife are in Wadena, Minn.

Miss Mollie Moore was married recently to Lt. Varnum of the famous 7th. cavalry and the bridal couple are now living at Ft. Yates, where the lieutenant is now stationed.

Mrs. Josie Maxwell nee Smith, is visiting her husband's parents in Port Byron, Il'.

Tommy Smith is wintering in Deadwood. He will return to the British Possessions in the spring.

Kirby Garner and family are in the southern Black Hills.

Chas. Brown, formerly a partner of John Warn in the "Oyster Grotto," is in Oppelo, Kansas.

P. S. Bemis is on a cow ranch in Arizona, but has not yet sent us his address.

"Reno" Marsh is hunting for a fur company in Alaska.

John Munro is owner of the Æ brand of cattle and is living on Beaver creek, above Mingusville.

"Dynamite" Jimmy McShane is a prominent official of the road, with headquarters at Sully Springs.

Johnny Chute was last heard of in Helena.

Mrs. John Anderson is in Rapid City. She wishes information concerning the whereabouts of her son, Charles Williams.

J. B. Prior is running a shoe shop in Dickinson.

George Wilkes and family are in London, England, where George is running a machine shop.

"Scotty" Beaumont was married recently in London, England.
articles.summary: Roundup of the whereabouts of former Medora-area residents, including A. W. Merrifield, wintering in Canada.

articles.headline: The Cattle Interests.
articles.text:
DENVER, Col., Nov. 30.—The following letter was addressed to President Cleveland to-day:

OFFICE OF THE INTERNATIONAL RANGE ASSOCIATION, DENVER, Col., Nov. 30.—His Excellency, Grover Cleveland, President of the United States: The time has come when that branch of the commercial interest of our country represented by the live stock industry feels that it should no longer plead for, but demand justice. I am empowered by the live stock men of the plains, who have more than $600,000,000 invested in cattle, to respectfully invite the attention of Your Excellency to the imminent danger threatening our herds by the existence of contagious bovine diseases, which, if once introduced to the open ranges west, will sweep our entire interests from the earth. I feel that I am justified in asking that in your forthcoming message to Congress some suggestions may be made in the interest of legislation looking to the extermination of the contagious cattle disease known as pleuro-pneumonia, and such sanitary regulations as will protect the cattle interest of the United States against the importation of cattle from known disease centers of other countries.

I would further respectfully submit that under the pooling system entered into by the transportation companies of the United States, and the iniquitous favoritism of the rebate system, grievous wrongs are perpetrated on the producer of beef and the consumer as well. That same combination which compels the millions who toil to pay an exorbitant price ior one of the prime necessaries of life, compels the producer to accept for his products a price which has pressed the cattle-growers to the verge of ruin. The bill now pending before Congress for the regulation of inter-state commerce, known as the Reagan bill, is in the interest of justice and equity, and the cattle industry bespeaks for it such attention in your message as may meet your commendation. Respectfully,

R. G. HEAD,

President Internationl Range Association.
articles.summary: International Range Association president R. G. Head asks President Cleveland to back pleuro-pneumonia legislation and the Reagan interstate commerce bill.

articles.headline: A Festive Cow Puncher.
articles.text:
Cowboys as a class are brimful and running over with wit, merriment, good humor. They are always ready for any bit of innocent fun, but are not perpetually spoiling for a fight, as has so often been said of them. They are at peace with all men, and would not be otherwise from choice. As a rule, if a man quarrels with one of them, he forces the war, and is himself to blame. Their love for fun often leads to trouble, though generally because the victim of it does not know how or is not willing to either "clip in' or excuse himself. They are fond of "piping off" anything that is conspicuous, or vice versa, no matter to whom it belongs, and they dislike to see snobbish airs assumed in their country, though such might pass current in any eastern city.

I once saw a dude step out of a hotel in Cheyenne wearing a silk hat, lavender trousers, cut-away coat, high pressure collar, scarlet velvet scarf, patent-leather shoes, etc. Several cowboys were riding through the street, and spied him.

"Say, Dick," said one of them, "what do ye 'spose it is!"

"Let's tackle it and see," said Dick. "It looks alive."

"Let's brand it," said Dick, and as quick as a flash a riata fell about the dude, closed around his slender waist and he was a prisoner. The boys gathered around him, chaffed him good naturedly, took his hat rubbed the nap the wrong way, put some alkali mud on his shoes, and then releasing him and bidding him "go in and put on some clothes," rode off. A good natured repartee on his part, or an invitation to drink or smoke, or a pleasant reply of any kind would have "let him out" without any unpleasant treatment; but he scorned them, and they considered it a duty to society to post him on how to act away from home.

In common with all other human beings, the cowboys require and must have amusement of some kind, and his isolated condition depriving him of the privilege of theaters, parties, billiards and other varieties of amusement that young men in the states usually indulge in, it is but natural that his exuberance of spirits should cause him to find sport of other kinds. His only sources of amusement on the ranch are his rifle, revolver, broncho, lariat, and cards, and in course of time he tires of these and seeks a change.

He goes to town and meets there some of his comrades or acquaintances, and they indulge in some wild pranks which to eastern people, and especially those who happen to fall victims to their practical jokes, appear ruffianly. Their love of excitement and adventure sometimes gets the better of their judgement and they carry their fun to excess. They corral the crew of a [train?] which has stopped at a station, and [amuse?] themselves and the passengers by making the conductor, brakeman, baggagemen, engineer, and fireman dance a jig to the music of sixshooters. In one instance they boarded a train, and made the Theodore Thomas orchestra give them an extemporaneous concert. They have been known to carry their revels to still worse excesses than these, and to resort to acts of real abuse and injury against defenseless people. But such acts on the part of genuine cowboys are rare, and are rigorously condemned by all respectable elements in the business. I would much rather take my chances as to safety of life and property in a country inhabited only by cowboys than in any eastern town or city, with all its police "protection."

An incident may serve to illustrate how suddenly eastern people change their opinions of cowboys on close acquaintance. I was going west a few years since on the Northern Pacific railroad, and stepping off the train at Dickinson, Dakota, I met Howard Eaton, an old-time friend and fellow hunter, a typical cowboy, who has charge of a ranch and a herd of cattle in the "bad lands" on the Little Missouri river. He was dressed in the regulation costume of the craft—canvas trousers and jacket, leather chaparajoes, blue flannel shirt and broad-brimmed white felt hat. His loins were girt about with a well-filled cartridge belt, from which hung his six-shooter—a weapon that may almost be termed a badge of the order. Large Mexican spurs rattled at his heels as he walked. He had ridden thirty-five miles under the spur, arriving at the station just in time to catch the train, and having no time to change his apparel, even if he had wished to do so. He was going some distance on the same train, and I invited him into the sleeper. As he entered and walked down the aisle the passengers became suddenly alarmed, imagining that the train had been corralled by a party of the terrible cowboys; but when I conducted him to our section and introduced him to my wife, they began to feel easier. We had a well-filled lunch basket with us, and my wife hastily spread its contents before him. He ate as only a cowboy can eat. Our fellow-passengers became interested spectators, and after our friend had finished his repast we introduced him to several of them. They were agreeably surprised at his polished manners, his fluent and well-chosen language, his handsome though sun-browned face, and his kind genial nature—at finding, in fact, that he was an educated and cultivated gentleman. Before we had been an hour together they had learned to respect and admire the wild, picturesque character whom at first they had feared.

Altogether, cow-boys are a whole-souled, large-hearted generous class of fellows, whom it is a pleasure to ride with, eat with, and associate with; and it is safe to say that nine-tenths of the hard things that have been said of them have come from men who never knew intimately a single one of them. I contend that a year spent on the hurricane deck of a cow-pony is one of the most useful and valuable pieces of experience a young man can possibly have in fitting himself for business of almost any kind; and if I were educating a boy to fight the battle of life, I would secure him a cowboy's situation as soon as he was through with his studies at school. A term of service on a frontier cattle-ranch will take the conceit out of any boy; it will at the same time teach him self reliance; it will teach him to endure hardships and suffering; will give nerve and pluck; it will develop the latent energy in him to a degree that could not be accomplished by any other apprenticeship or experience I know of. Many of the successful business men of the western towns of to-day, served their first years on the frontier as "cow-punchers," and to that school they owe the firmness of character and the ability to surmount great obstacles that have made their success in life possible.

I contend that the constant communion with nature, the study of her broad, pure domains, the days and nights of lonely cruising and camping on the prairie, the uninterrupted communion with and study of self which this occupation affords, tend to make young men honest and noble, much more so than the same men would be if deprived of these opportunities, confined to the limits of our boasted "civilization,' and compelled to breathe constantly the air of adroitness, of strategy, of competition, of suspicion and crime. If every young man reared in the town or city could have the advantages of a year or of constant study of nature, we should have more honest men.—G. O. Shields in Harpers Weekly.
articles.summary: Reprint of G. O. Shields's Harper's Weekly defense of cowboys, featuring an anecdote about Howard Eaton of the Bad Lands boarding a train at Dickinson.

articles.text: Unless the circuit court reverses the decision of election commissioners of Stark county, Morris Sebastian is elected sheriff of Stark county by a majority of four votes.
articles.summary: Morris Sebastian elected Stark County sheriff by four votes, pending possible court reversal.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts has been travelling about so much that it is hard to keep track of him. He was last heard from in Cheyenne, where he was buying stock.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts is in Cheyenne buying stock.

articles.text: It seems altogether likely that the experiment of raising sheep will again be tried in the Bad Lands. From present indications, at least two flocks will be turned in next spring.
articles.summary: At least two sheep flocks expected in the Bad Lands next spring.

articles.text: The beautiful weather we have been having lately is a constant and always new source of wonder even to the oldest settlers. The cold snap will probably strike us about the holidays.
articles.summary: Unusually fine weather continues; a cold snap expected around the holidays.

articles.text: Everyone here will remember the pretty face and sunny disposition of little Gussie O'Hara. There will be many sincere mourners here at the news of his death, which occurred this week in St. Paul.
articles.summary: Little Gussie O'Hara, remembered in Medora, died this week in St. Paul.

articles.text: Our congratulations last week on the marriage or approaching marriage of Riley Brooks and Miss Lilly Roberts, were not premature. They were married in Dickinson last Wednesday and for the present at least, will reside in Medora.

articles.headline: Commissioners' Meeting.
articles.text:
A special meeting of the board of county commissioners of Billings county, was held Nov. 27, 1886.

Meeting called to order by the chairman of the board.

Present: Commissioners Truscott and Goodall and Clerk Williamson.

The first business before the board was to consider the bills on file against the county.

Dr. Wm. A. Bentley was allowed for attendance on Billings county poor, the sum of fifty-one dollars.

The N. P. Ref. Car Co. was allowed $19.90 for removing jail cells.

B. J. VanVleck was allowed six dollars for services rendered in the organization of Billings county.

J. C. Williamson was allowed for stationery and [postage?] furnished the county, $5.45.

J. C. Williamson, county clerk, was allowed his expenses while assisting in the canvass of the vote for councilman and members of the Assembly, at the senior county, Burleigh, thirty-three dollars.

George D. Barnard was allowed six dollars for stationery.

W. T. Dantz was allowed for supplies furnished and services rendered as Sup't. of schools, $50.98.

On motion, the board adjourned.

J. C. WILLIAMSON, County Clerk.
articles.summary: Proceedings of the Billings County commissioners' special meeting of Nov. 27, 1886, allowing bills against the county.

events.title: Chicago cattle receipts fall to 7,000 head
events.summary: The paper reported that Monday's cattle receipts at the Chicago yards were 7,000 head against 14,000 the Monday before, with generally poor quality.
events.excerpt: Monday's receipts of cattle in the Chicago yards amounted to 7,000 head, against 14,000 received the previous Monday.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Cow Boy urges repeal of territorial exemption laws
events.summary: In an editorial the Cow Boy argued that the $1,500 property exemption from debt was too high by at least $1,200 and hoped the coming legislature would repeal or reduce it.
events.excerpt: A total abolishment of the exemption laws would be far preferable to the present ones

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Rumors of two more marriages
events.summary: The paper reported numerous rumors that two more marriages were about to take place.
events.excerpt: There are numerous rumors of two more marriages about to take place.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Ice harvest delayed; river not frozen thick enough
events.summary: Work on cutting ice was to begin the following week, but the ice was not yet thick enough.
events.excerpt: it is not yet frozen to a sufficient thickness.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Mrs. D. K. Wade visiting her mother in New Brighton, Pa.
events.summary: The paper corrected last week's report: Mrs. D. K. Wade was in New Brighton, Pennsylvania, visiting her mother, not in Faribault, Minnesota.
events.excerpt: She is in New Brighton, Penn., visiting her mother.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: A. W. Merrifield wintering at his old Canadian home
events.summary: Among news of old-timers, the paper reported that A. W. Merrifield was at his old home in Canada and would return in the spring.
events.excerpt: A. W. Merrifield is in his old Canadian home and will return in the spring.

events.date_basis: "married recently", no date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Mollie Moore marries Lt. Varnum of the 7th Cavalry
events.summary: Former resident Miss Mollie Moore was reported recently married to Lt. Varnum of the 7th Cavalry; the couple was living at Fort Yates.
events.excerpt: Miss Mollie Moore was married recently to Lt. Varnum of the famous 7th. cavalry

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Whereabouts of Medora old-timers reported
events.summary: The Cow Boy listed where former residents had gone: Al. Gifford in Miles City, Tommy Smith in Deadwood, P. S. Bemis ranching in Arizona, "Reno" Marsh hunting furs in Alaska, J. B. Prior running a shoe shop in Dickinson, George Wilkes in London, and others.
events.excerpt: J. B. Prior is running a shoe shop in Dickinson.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Mrs. John Anderson seeks her son Charles Williams
events.summary: Mrs. John Anderson of Rapid City asked through the paper for information about the whereabouts of her son, Charles Williams.
events.excerpt: She wishes information concerning the whereabouts of her son, Charles Williams.

events.date_basis: Dateline Denver, Nov. 30
events.title: Range Association petitions Cleveland on cattle disease and railroad rates
events.summary: R. G. Head, president of the International Range Association, wrote President Cleveland asking for legislation against pleuro-pneumonia and support for the Reagan interstate commerce bill.
events.excerpt: the imminent danger threatening our herds by the existence of contagious bovine diseases

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Harper's Weekly sketch praising Howard Eaton reprinted
events.summary: The Cow Boy reprinted G. O. Shields's Harper's Weekly article on cowboys, which described meeting Howard Eaton, a Bad Lands cattleman, at Dickinson and how train passengers came to admire him; a local note teased Eaton about it.
events.excerpt: I met Howard Eaton, an old-time friend and fellow hunter, a typical cowboy, who has charge of a ranch and a herd of cattle in the "bad lands"

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Cow Boy offers Huffmann's round-up photographs
events.summary: The Cow Boy advertised its remaining sets of Huffmann's 36 instantaneous round-up photographs for $5, or $6 with a year's subscription.
events.excerpt: We have remaining a few sets of Huffmann's instantaneous round-up views, representing the most interesting events of the range cattle industry.

events.date_basis: "Friday" before Thu 9 Dec 1886
events.title: Johnny Goodall leaves for San Antonio
events.summary: Johnny Goodall left Friday morning for San Antonio, Texas, on business for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company.
events.excerpt: Johnny Goodall left Friday morning for San Antonio, Texas

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: L. W. Murch tips over a load of hay
events.summary: Tipping over hay loads had become common lately, and L. W. Murch was the latest to do so.
events.excerpt: L. W. Murch is the latest victim.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Herd of 400 antelope near Medora
events.summary: A herd of about four hundred antelope was ranging between Medora and the prairie north of the railroad track.
events.excerpt: There is a herd of about four hundred antelope, ranging between Medora and the prairie

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Ed. Turners go to Oregon
events.summary: Mr. and Mrs. Ed. Turner, who had been visiting in Terry until a few days before, were now in Oregon.
events.excerpt: Mr. and Mrs. Ed. Turner are now in Oregon.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Ice houses readied for the ice crop
events.summary: Work cleaning the ice houses and laying slides to the dam was nearly finished in readiness for the ice harvest.
events.excerpt: laying slides to the dam will soon be completed in readiness for the ice crop.

events.date_basis: "last Friday" before Thu 9 Dec 1886
events.title: Johnny McAdam sees 1,500 antelope
events.summary: Johnny McAdam stated that he saw 1,500 antelope on Friday.
events.excerpt: he saw 1,500 antelope last Friday.

events.date_basis: "last Friday" before Thu 9 Dec 1886
events.title: Chas. Ellison leaves to ready re-icing stations
events.summary: Chas. Ellison left for Kansas City to put in order the re-icing stations between there and New York for the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company.
events.excerpt: to put in order the re-icing stations between that point and New York

events.date_basis: "last Thursday, Friday and Saturday" before Thu 9 Dec 1886
events.title: Paddock and McGregor kill 37 antelope
events.summary: E. G. Paddock and J. A. McGregor killed thirty-seven antelope over Thursday, Friday and Saturday, besides many others.
events.excerpt: They killed thirty-seven last Thursday, Friday and Saturday

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Morris Sebastian elected Stark County sheriff by four votes
events.summary: Unless the circuit court reversed the election commissioners, Morris Sebastian was elected sheriff of Stark County by four votes.
events.excerpt: Morris Sebastian is elected sheriff of Stark county by a majority of four votes.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Lloyd Roberts buying stock in Cheyenne
events.summary: Lloyd Roberts of the Sloping Bottom ranch was last heard from in Cheyenne, buying stock.
events.excerpt: He was last heard from in Cheyenne, where he was buying stock.

events.date_basis: "next spring" after Thu 9 Dec 1886
events.title: Sheep raising to be tried again in the Bad Lands
events.summary: The paper expected the sheep-raising experiment to be tried again, with at least two flocks to be turned in next spring.
events.excerpt: at least two flocks will be turned in next spring.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Mild early-December weather amazes settlers
events.summary: The fine weather was described as a wonder even to the oldest settlers, with a cold snap expected about the holidays.
events.excerpt: The beautiful weather we have been having lately is a constant and always new source of wonder

events.date_basis: "this week", issue Thu 9 Dec 1886
events.title: Death of little Gussie O'Hara
events.summary: Little Gussie O'Hara, fondly remembered in Medora, died this week in St. Paul.
events.excerpt: There will be many sincere mourners here at the news of his death

events.date_basis: "last Wednesday" before Thu 9 Dec 1886
events.title: Riley Brooks and Lilly Roberts marry
events.summary: Riley Brooks and Miss Lilly Roberts were married in Dickinson and planned to live in Medora for the present.
events.excerpt: They were married in Dickinson last Wednesday and for the present at least, will reside in Medora.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Jack Tisdale and wife keeping house at the Elkhorn ranch
events.summary: In answer to inquiries about his whereabouts, the paper reported that Jack Tisdale and his wife were keeping house at the Elkhorn ranch.
events.excerpt: Jack Tisdale and wife are keeping house at the Elkhorn ranch.

events.date_basis: Stated: held Nov. 27, 1886
events.title: Billings County commissioners allow bills at special meeting
events.summary: Billings County commissioners Truscott and Goodall met and allowed bills, including $51 to Dr. Wm. A. Bentley for care of the county poor, $19.90 to the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. for removing jail cells, and $50.98 to W. T. Dantz as school superintendent.
events.excerpt: The N. P. Ref. Car Co. was allowed $19.90 for removing jail cells.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Packard closes out Studebaker wagon stock
events.summary: A. T. Packard advertised that he would sell his remaining Studebaker wagons for cash below wholesale factory rates to close out the stock.
events.excerpt: To close out the stock of Studebaker wagons now on hand, I will make prices for cash that are lower than the wholesale factory rate.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 9 Dec 1886 issue
events.title: Chimney Butte Ranch brand card lists Theodore Roosevelt as proprietor
events.summary: The paper's standing brand directory carried the Chimney Butte Ranch card naming Theodore Roosevelt as proprietor and Ferris & Merrifield as managers, P.O. Medora, with range six miles south of the Northern Pacific on the Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: CHIMNEY BUTTE RANCH. THEODORE ROOSEVELT, Proprietor. FERRIS & MERRIFIELD, Managers.
